method: Researched and written with web-search verification; then fact-checked independently by a second agent (WebSearch was available and was used for the Lawrence et al. 2013 and Grotzinger et al. 2014 citations, Brown & Schaller 2007, the IAU 2006 resolutions, 2025 moon counts and the naming of 1992 QB1; direct page fetches of NASA, NSSDCA, IAU and Crossref failed, so planetary fact-sheet values, mission dates and the Ottewell distances were checked by expert review and recomputed by hand, e.g. 1 inch = 100,000 miles gives 10, 19, 26, 39–40, 134–135, 246–247, 496, 776–777 and 1,019 yards; all SVG radii and positions were measured against their stated scales); every answer key re-solved blind.

corrections.quote: In 1992 David Jewitt and Jane Luu found a small object beyond Neptune, now called 1992 QB1,
corrections.correction: In 1992 David Jewitt and Jane Luu found a small object beyond Neptune, first designated 1992 QB1 and now named Albion,
corrections.why: The object received the official name (15760) Albion in January 2018; 1992 QB1 is its provisional designation, so 'now called 1992 QB1' is out of date. Discovery year and discoverers are correct (Jewitt & Luu 1993, Nature 362, 730–732).

corrections.quote: Dwarf planets are far too faint to see without a large telescope, and Jupiter’s moons look like sharp points beside Jupiter.
corrections.correction: Dwarf planets look like faint, star-like points with no tail, and most need a telescope; Jupiter’s moons look like sharp points beside Jupiter.
corrections.why: Ceres, a dwarf planet named in this same section, reaches about magnitude 6.7 at favorable oppositions and is easy in ordinary binoculars, so 'far too faint to see without a large telescope' is false for it. The key (A, comet) is still correct; the distinguishing clue is the fuzzy coma and tail.

corrections.quote: NASA’s Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, and in 2005 it dropped the European Huygens probe onto Saturn’s largest moon, Titan.
corrections.correction: NASA’s Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, and the European Huygens probe it carried landed on Saturn’s largest moon, Titan, in January 2005.
corrections.why: Cassini released Huygens on 25 December 2004; Huygens descended and landed on 14 January 2005. 'In 2005 it dropped' puts the release in the wrong year; stating the landing date is accurate and consistent with the 2.3 reading.

corrections.quote: The four rocky planets crowd within about 1.5 AU of the Sun, while each giant planet lies one and a half to two times as far out as the one before it, and the Kuiper Belt begins near Neptune’s orbit.
corrections.correction: The four rocky planets crowd within about 1.5 AU of the Sun, Jupiter lies more than three times as far out as Mars, each later giant planet lies one and a half to two times as far out as the one before it, and the Kuiper Belt begins near Neptune’s orbit.
corrections.why: The planet before Jupiter is Mars, and 5.2 / 1.52 ≈ 3.4, not 1.5–2. The 1.5–2 ratio holds only for Saturn/Jupiter (1.84), Uranus/Saturn (2.0) and Neptune/Uranus (1.57). The slide notes already say Jupiter is more than three times as far as Mars.

corrections.quote: Ganymede and Titan are wider than Mercury, and seven moons are larger than Pluto, which is why size is not one of the tests the IAU uses to define a planet.
corrections.correction: Ganymede and Titan are wider than Mercury, and seven moons are larger than Pluto, which shows that size alone does not decide whether a body is a planet.
corrections.why: The IAU resolution gives no such reason, so 'which is why' invents a motive. It also sits awkwardly with criterion (b), which is a size-related (mass) condition, as the 2.3 misconception itself says. The arithmetic is right: Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, the Moon, Europa and Triton are all wider than Pluto's 2,377 km.

corrections.quote: Then calculate the exact positions (distance in AU ÷ 39.5 × 100 cm) for all eight planets, the asteroid belt and Neptune, mark them, and compare them with your folds.
corrections.correction: Then calculate the exact positions (distance in AU ÷ 39.5 × 100 cm) for all eight planets and the edges of the asteroid belt, mark them, and compare them with your folds.
corrections.why: Neptune is one of the eight planets, so listing it again is redundant and confusing for a beginner. The arithmetic in the rubric is correct (belt 5.6–8.1 cm, Neptune 76 cm, Mars 3.85 cm; folds at 19.75, 9.9 and 4.9 AU land near Uranus, Saturn and Jupiter).

corrections.quote: Chapters 12 and 13: the Galilean moons, Titan, Triton, Enceladus, Pluto, asteroids, meteors, comets, meteor showers and the Oort Cloud.
corrections.correction: Chapters 12 to 14: the Galilean moons, Titan, Triton, Enceladus, Pluto, asteroids, meteors, comets, meteor showers and the Oort Cloud.
corrections.why: In OpenStax Astronomy 2e, meteors and meteor showers are covered in Chapter 14 (Cosmic Samples and the Origin of the Solar System, section 14.1 Meteors), not in Chapters 12 or 13.

corrections.quote: Lawrence, D. J., Feldman, W. C., Goldsten, J. O., Maurice, S., Peplowski, P. N., Anderson, B. W., . . . Solomon, S. C. (2013).
corrections.correction: Lawrence, D. J., Feldman, W. C., Goldsten, J. O., Maurice, S., Peplowski, P. N., et al. (2013).
corrections.why: Web search confirmed the paper is real: David J. Lawrence (APL) is lead author, Feldman and Prettyman are co-authors, the title matches, and it appeared in Science after release on Science Express in November 2012. Volume 339, issue 6117, pages 292–296 fit the companion papers (Neumann et al. 339:296; Paige et al. 339:300). The tail of the author list could not be checked. From memory, the sixth author is Brian J. Anderson, not 'B. W.', and the final author is S. Z. Weider, not Solomon, so in APA ellipsis style the name after '. . .' is probably wrong. Shorten the list rather than guess.

summary: The chapter is highly accurate. All planet diameters, distances, periods, densities, Ottewell model distances, moon counts as of 2025, IAU criteria, mission dates and figure scales checked out, and all 14 multiple-choice keys are correct. The fixes are small: an outdated name for 1992 QB1, an overstatement that dwarf planets need a large telescope (Ceres does not), a wrong ratio in the Figure 2 caption, a Huygens date slip, an invented IAU motive in the Figure 3 caption, a redundant phrase in a challenge, a mis-cited OpenStax chapter range, and an uncertain author tail in the Lawrence et al. citation.
